newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas trade talks not seen reaching consensus.
newsitem.headline: Americas trade talks not seen reaching consensus.

text.p: Deputy trade ministers from 34 countries in the Americas are unlikely to reach on Thursday a consensus in talks on setting up a free trade zone stretching from Alaska to the plains of Patagonia, a Brazilian official said.

Jose Artur Denot Medeiros, Brazil's envoy to the Latin American Aladi group, said "unless the Holy Spirit descends", officials meeting in Rio de Janeiro would probably not drum up an agreement for a May 15-16 ministerial summit in the Brazilian city of Belo Horizonte.

"Our evaluation is that we probably won't be able to conclude the Ministerial Declaration for Belo Horizonte ... unless something happens this afternoon like the Holy Spirit descending," Medeiros said in a midday briefing.
Leaders of 34 countries in the region, excluding Cuba, decided at the 1994 Miami summit to set up the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) by the year 2005.

Deputy trade ministers were due to conclude Thursday four days of preparatory talks in Rio de Janeiro ahead of the May ministerial meeting, which will be followed by another pow-wow of ministers in Costa Rica next February and a presidential summit in Santiago, Chile, in March.
Medeiros said continuing disagreements did not mean Belo Horizonte would be a "failure".
"This hasn't caused surprise, disappointment. None of that. This is just the normal process of international negotiations," he said.
The Brazilian official said the talks had got stuck on the crucial issue of what timetable negotiations should follow and what structure they should take.
All FTAA signatory countries agreed that formal talks should be launched after the Santiago summit.

But Mercosur, grouping Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, are insisting on three stages, starting with "business facilitation", basically the eradication of bureaucratic barriers to trade, followed by subsidies and then finally the thorny issue of tariff reductions.
Canada and the United States want to discuss all aspects of trade liberalization at the same time, a suggestion Medeiros equated to "launching negotiations into a vacuum".

"We need to know exactly what these negotiations are going to be," he said, saying the Andean Pact coubtries and even Washington's Nafta partner Mexico seemed to agree with the timing aspect of the Mercosur position.

For Belo Horizonte, Brazil expected Rio to come up with a declaration that included alternatives to certain paragraphs. An eve-of-summit gathering of deputies in Belo Horizonte was also a possibility.

Though stressing that "great advances" had been made in Rio, in particular by coming up with "the structure" of the Ministerial Declaration if not its substance, Medeiros acknowledged there was some risk of a fiasco in Belo Horizonte.
"Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed," he said, adding that without an accord by the time the Santiago summit comes around, formal FTAA negotiations would not start in 1998.
